findings.headline: Homes England strategic partnership bid outcome pending, with £2.5m reserve set aside for local government reorganisation transitional costs but actual costs remain highly uncertain
findings.detail: The 30-Year HRA Business Plan assumes success in Homes England bid for strategic partnership to unlock significant capital grant funding. Outcome expected shortly and will require business plan refresh. Separately, LGR transitional costs are estimated at £2.5m reserve but actual costs remain highly uncertain with risks from staff turnover and recruitment impacts.
findings.matters: HRA financial plan hinges on grant funding from uncertain bid outcome. LGR transitional costs are contingent and could exceed reserve if staff turnover accelerates or labour market tightens.
findings.figures: £2.5m reserve for LGR transitional costs; grant funding amount unquantified
findings.quote: the 2026/27 BSR and 30-Year Business Plan assumes that the council will be successful in its bid to Homes England for a strategic partnership which will unlock significant capital grant funding. The outcome of this bid is expected shortly

findings.headline: Review of asset compliance across operational estate likely to identify significant unbudgeted immediate capital works requirements
findings.detail: Ongoing review of asset compliance across the council's operational estate is expected to identify immediate requirements for capital works and remediation described as likely to be significant, though the amount is not yet quantified.
findings.matters: Unquantified but material capital demands emerging outside the planned capital programme threaten both borrowing capacity and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Amount described as 'likely to be significant' but unquantified
findings.quote: The ongoing review of asset compliance across the council's operational estate is likely to identify some immediate requirements for capital works and remediation, which may be significant.

findings.headline: Business rates income shortfall of £1.0m in 2025-26 outturn, with baseline reset removing all previously accumulated growth and significant revaluation appeals pending
findings.detail: 2025/26 Outturn Report shows business rates income shortfall of almost £1.0m. 2026 revaluation generated significant rating appeals, and baseline reset removed all previously accumulated business rates growth. Uncertainty remains on whether forecast income levels can be achieved, though there is both downside and upside risk.
findings.matters: Business rates are a core revenue source; a £1m actual shortfall against budget signals either forecast error or volatile income stream. Future growth potential uncertain following baseline reset.
findings.figures: £1.0m shortfall in 2025-26; all business rates growth reset to zero
findings.quote: there remains significant uncertainty around business rates income following the 2026 revaluation (which has generated significant rating appeals) and baseline reset (which has removed all previously accumulated business rates growth)... the 2025/26 Outturn Report shows a shortfall in business rates income of almost £1.0 million.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account reported £6.9m net operating overspend in 2025-26, mainly repairs and maintenance with Awaab's Law adding significant damp/mould/condensation pressures
findings.detail: 2025/26 HRA overspend of £6.9m driven by repairs and maintenance overspends. Implementation of Awaab's Law has significantly increased costs, particularly around damp, condensation and mould. Void costs remain significantly higher than benchmarks. One-off fire safety waking watch and insurance incidents also contributed.
findings.matters: HRA overspends force increased council borrowing to fund the new build housing programme, raising debt costs and crowding out other investment. Demand-led and structural cost drivers are unlikely to reduce soon despite additional £1.7m budget allocation.
findings.figures: £6.9m 2025-26 net operating overspend; additional £1.7m per year allocated in 2026-27 BSR
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the HRA reported a net operating overspend of £6.9 million. This was mainly due to overspends on repairs and maintenance. The implementation of Awaab's Law has significantly added to cost pressures in this area, particularly around damp, condensation and mould (DCM).

findings.headline: Greater Cambridge Development Corporation will take planning powers and is likely to cause significant financial pressure including redundancy costs and loss of planning income
findings.detail: Government published its response to consultation on establishing a new development corporation for Greater Cambridge in June 2026. The proposal will hand some planning powers to the Development Corporation, likely causing costs for potential redundancies and/or TUPE arrangements, plus loss of a significant portion of the council's planning income.
findings.matters: Loss of planning income is a structural reduction in revenue capacity, combined with unquantified redundancy costs, both reducing available revenue for debt service and service delivery.
findings.figures: Planning income loss described as 'significant portion', redundancy/TUPE costs undefined
findings.quote: Whilst the full details are not yet known, this is likely to cause significant financial pressures for the council, including costs associated with potential redundancies and/or TUPE arrangements. It is also likely that the council will lose a significant portion of its planning income in the future.

findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rates increased from 5.55% assumption to 6.16% actual, with £45.8m external borrowing forecast for 2025-26
findings.detail: The Budget Setting Report assumed average PWLB borrowing rates of 5.55% for 2025/26, but the rate as at 29 June 2026 is 6.16%. With external borrowing forecast at £45.8m, even small rate increases have lasting impact on budgets. Increased costs may also pressure capital projects including new build housing and Civic Quarter.
findings.matters: Higher borrowing costs reduce capital programme viability and increase ongoing debt service costs, constraining financial flexibility for a council requiring significant external borrowing.
findings.figures: £45.8m external borrowing forecast; rates moved from 5.55% to 6.16% (61 basis point increase)
findings.quote: The BSR assumed an average PWLB borrowing rates for 2025/26 of 5.55%, however the current equivalent rate as at 29 June 2026 is 6.16%... given the extent of external borrowing required in 2025/26 (forecast at £45.8 million in the BSR), even a small increase in rates will have a lasting effect on the council's budgets.

findings.headline: CPI inflation forecast at 3.6% for 2026, exceeding budget assumption of 2.6% by a full percentage point
findings.detail: HM Treasury's latest independent forecasts show CPI at 3.6% for calendar year 2026, which will feed into 2027-28 pricing. The council's budget assumed 2.6% inflation. A comparable inflation shock last year increased the five-year savings target by almost £1.0m.
findings.matters: Inflation above budget erodes buying power on a fixed revenue base, directly forcing either greater savings or deeper borrowing.
findings.figures: Forecast 3.6% CPI vs 2.6% budget assumption; prior similar movement added £1.0m to five-year targets
findings.quote: The latest independent forecasts published by HM Treasury show CPI inflation at 3.6% for the 2026 calendar year, which will feed directly into 2027/28 prices. For context, a similar movement in forecast inflation rates last year increased the five-year savings target by almost £1.0 million.

findings.headline: Savings targets anticipated to increase materially from original £0.375m forecast for 2027-28
findings.detail: The Budget Setting Report 2026/27 set cumulative savings targets of £0.375m for 2027-28, but emerging pressures and updated economic forecasts mean targets will be refreshed upward. A similar inflation movement last year increased five-year targets by almost £1.0m.
findings.matters: Rising savings requirements signal deteriorating financial sustainability and constrained revenue to service debt or invest in capital programmes.
findings.figures: Original target £0.375m for 2027-28; prior year inflation shock added £1.0m to five-year targets
findings.quote: it is currently anticipated that savings targets will increase, for the reasons set out below

findings.headline: Loss of income streams: crematorium income declining due to new providers and online direct cremation services
findings.detail: The budget cites 'Loss of crematorium income from new providers and online-direct cremation services' and 'decline in retail rents at Lion Yard' as material budget pressures being absorbed.
findings.matters: These reflect structural market changes reducing the council's income base. They are permanent losses, not temporary pressures, and suggest further income streams may be vulnerable to market disruption.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the document
findings.quote: Loss of crematorium income from new providers and online-direct cremation services; decline in retail rents at Lion Yard

findings.headline: £2.5 million earmarked reserve set aside for local government reorganisation costs, with council's share of £19.0 million transition spend yet to be determined
findings.detail: The council has set aside £2.5 million 'as an early prudent estimate of this council's likely required contribution' to the estimated £57.4 million total reorganisation costs across the seven predecessor authorities. The final allocation method has not yet been agreed.
findings.matters: The true cost to Cambridge of merging into a unitary authority is unknown and the funding mechanism is undefined. The £2.5 million may be insufficient. This adds further uncertainty to medium-term finances and could force additional borrowing or service cuts.
findings.figures: £2.5 million set aside; estimated £57.4 million total reorganisation costs across 7 authorities; £19.0 million to be spent pre-vesting day
findings.quote: This BSR sets aside £2.5 million into an earmarked reserve for local government reorganisation

findings.headline: HRA rent convergence programme to commence April 2027, increasing rents above 4.8% for below-formula tenants
findings.detail: The council has 'set out our intention to implement a programme of rent convergence for council tenants who are currently paying below formula rent due to historic below-inflation cost capping, to commence in April 2027.' This is expected to generate £1.4 million per year by 2030/31 and is critical to funding the identified £2.2 million in HRA pressures.
findings.matters: This is a material change to tenant finances dependent on successful implementation. If convergence is delayed or softened due to tenant resistance or affordability concerns, it will leave a £1.4 million funding gap in the HRA. The council is relying on this income to balance.
findings.figures: Expected to generate £1.4 million per year by 2030/31
findings.quote: Much of this investment will be funded through rent convergence, which is expected to generate an additional £1.4 million per year by 2030/31. This will see the rents of households who currently pay less than social formula rent gradually increase (over a number of years) until the correct level is met

findings.headline: Damp, mould, and compliance costs adding £750,000 per year to HRA baseline
findings.detail: The budget includes 'an additional £750,000 per year to address damp, condensation and mould, supporting full compliance with Awaab's Law.' This was identified through the zero-based budgeting exercise and represents a permanent new cost pressure.
findings.matters: This is a reactive cost being added to a budget that is already overspending. It suggests either poor asset condition or that previous budgets systematically underestimated compliance costs for housing regulations. The council will be unable to absorb this from within existing HRA resources.
findings.figures: £750,000 per year additional cost
findings.quote: an additional £750,000 per year to address damp, condensation and mould, supporting full compliance with Awaab's Law

findings.headline: HRA debt of £230.4 million, with council planning to borrow significantly more for new build programme
findings.detail: As of 1 April 2025, HRA net debt stands at £230.4 million (£213.6 million external, £16.8 million internal). The council states 'the council is required to borrow significantly greater sums from 2025/26 onwards, particularly to fund its HRA new build development programme' and is exploring alternatives to PWLB borrowing.
findings.matters: The council faces substantial additional borrowing while PWLB rates remain elevated (over 6% for 25-year maturity), and while the HRA is still reporting operating deficits. The shift away from PWLB toward alternative routes (internal borrowing, inter-authority, market) suggests concern about rate sustainability.
findings.figures: £230.4 million HRA net debt; £213.6 million external PWLB debt
findings.quote: the council is required to borrow significantly greater sums from 2025/26 onwards, particularly to fund its HRA new build development programme. Consideration will be given to internal borrowing, inter-authority borrowing, market borrowing and institutional investment

findings.headline: Treasury investment income expected to decline as excess cash is deployed into capital programmes
findings.detail: The council currently benefits from high treasury income, but anticipates 'current high levels of income from the council's treasury management investments will significantly reduce over the next two years as the council's excess cash is invested in capital projects, and interest rates continue to fall.'
findings.matters: The council is dependent on volatile treasury returns to balance its budget (£53.4 million of £81.3 million gross budget is from fees, charges, and investment income). As cash is deployed and rates fall, this income buffer will disappear, tightening the finances precisely when borrowing needs are rising.
findings.figures: £53.4 million of £81.3 million total budget from fees, charges, commercial and investment income
findings.quote: An expectation that current high levels of income from the council's treasury management investments will significantly reduce over the next two years as the council's excess cash is invested in capital projects, and interest rates continue to fall

findings.headline: Core spending power declining 11.2% in real terms over three years despite headline inflation increases
findings.detail: Although national core spending power (CSP) grows nominally by 6.1% in 2026/27, Cambridge's own CSP decreases by 2.2% in 2026/27, falls 1.7% in 2027/28, then flatlines at 0% in 2028/29. Accounting for inflation, this represents a real-terms cut of 11.2% over three years, driven by fair funding reforms that penalised the council for accumulated business rates growth since 2013.
findings.matters: The council's funding is shrinking in real terms while inflation continues to erode service purchasing power. The loss of business rates growth accumulated since 2013 is permanent and removes a key income source.
findings.quote: the actual change in CSP the council will see is -2.2% in 2026/27, -1.7% in 2027/28, then 0.0% in 2028/29. Note that these figures are in cash terms – this represents a real term cut in CSP of around 11.2% over the next three years

findings.headline: Remaining 5-year budget gap of £1.4 million, with £0.4 million needed by 2027/28 before unitary restructure
findings.detail: The council identified a £3.6 million General Fund savings target for 2030/31 but has reduced it to £1.4 million through this year's budget measures. However, £0.4 million of savings still needs to be found by 2027/28, just before the planned local government reorganisation in April 2028.
findings.matters: An unsolved budget gap heading into a major organisational restructure creates refinancing and service continuity risk. The council will need to cut services or find new income while simultaneously integrating with South Cambridgeshire into a new unitary authority.
findings.figures: £1.4 million remaining gap by 2030/31; £0.4 million still needed by 2027/28
findings.quote: The five-year budget gap has now been reduced by £2.2 million, from £3.6 million to £1.4 million

findings.headline: HRA operating overspends have persisted across two years, requiring zero-based budget rewrite
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account reported an operating overspend of £2.3 million in 2024/25 and a further £3.1 million forecast for 2025/26. The council responded by conducting a zero-based budgeting exercise with external consultants to completely refresh the HRA budget and 30-Year Business Plan, suggesting the previous allocation framework was no longer reliable.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends in a ring-fenced housing account point to either forecasting failures or cost pressures the council has struggled to contain. The decision to scrap the existing budget structure indicates prior assumptions were significantly wrong.
findings.figures: £2.3 million overspend 2024/25; £3.1 million forecast overspend 2025/26
findings.quote: significant variances between allocated budgets and actual expenditure within the HRA, with an operating overspend of £2.3 million reported in 2024/25, and a further overspend of £3.1 million forecast for 2025/26

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridge City Council - Audit Results Report February 2026
findings.headline: Historic breach of rent-setting regulations on housing stock requiring tenant refunds
findings.detail: The council identified a historic breach of regulations relating to rental charges on its housing stock. The council misinterpreted how rent should be calculated and charged, leading to systematic overcharges to current and previous tenants. The council is required to refund these overpayments and has made a provision for this. While auditors concluded the financial statement impact was not material, this represents a breach of the Welfare Reform and Work Act 2016 and indicates control failures in housing revenue management.
findings.matters: A systematic breach of rent-setting regulations shows control failures in the council's housing operations and creates legal and reputational risk. The council is out of compliance with statutory duties.
findings.figures: Historic breach, current and previous tenants affected, provision made by council
findings.quote: The Council identified a historic breach of regulations relating to rental charges on housing stock. This involves misinterpretations in how rent has been calculated and charged, which has led to the overcharge of rent to some tenants. Consequently, the Council will need to refund overpayments of rent to current and previous tenants.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridge City Council - Audit Results Report February 2026
findings.headline: Investment Property valuations (£171 million) cannot be corroborated; rent data discrepancies with valuer
findings.detail: Auditors found discrepancies between rent data the council provided and information used by the external valuer. For three property samples, the council could not produce lease agreements to support the rent figures used in valuations. One valuation contained an error by the valuer using an incorrect combined income figure. Auditors could not complete planned procedures on this material balance because the council did not provide evidence within agreed timeframes.
findings.matters: Investment Property is Cambridge's largest asset class. If the council cannot produce lease agreements to verify rent income, valuations are unreliable. This indicates poor lease management and record-keeping on the council's most material asset.
findings.figures: £171 million Investment Property balance; £0.190 million overstatement identified; three properties with missing lease agreements
findings.quote: Our work identified discrepancies between the rent data provided by the Council and the information used by the valuer in their valuation calculations. For three samples, the Council was unable to provide lease agreements to corroborate the rent data used. We have been unable to complete our planned procedures for testing of Investment Property valuations as the Council have not provided corroborating evidence.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridge City Council - Audit Results Report February 2026
findings.headline: Five key audit procedures remain incomplete due to missing or inadequate evidence from the council
findings.detail: Auditors were unable to complete planned testing across five material areas. For fraud testing, the council provided no sample evidence for journal entries. For PPE additions, 20% of the tested sample had no corroborating evidence. For Investment Property valuations, the council did not provide corroborating evidence and lease agreements. For bad debt provision, no working papers or detailed debtors listing was provided. For IFRS 16 lease valuations, one assumption was based on forecasts rather than historical data with unclear basis.
findings.matters: Incomplete audit work across five material areas means key balances have not been verified. This is evidence of systemic problems in the council's record-keeping and financial processes.
findings.figures: Five audit areas with incomplete procedures; 20% of PPE sample unsupported; three Investment Property samples lacking lease agreements
findings.quote: We have been unable to complete our planned procedures in relation to testing of journal entries as Management was unable to provide evidence to support any of the selected sampled journal transactions. We have not completed our testing of Property, Plant, and Equipment (PPE) additions as the Council was unable to provide corroborating evidence to support 20% of the sampled transactions.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridge City Council - Audit Results Report February 2026
findings.headline: Finance team lacks capacity and expertise, identified as a significant VFM weakness in governance
findings.detail: Auditors have concluded there is a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements for securing value for money. The Finance Team lacks necessary expertise and capacity to produce good-quality financial information and supporting working papers. The primary finance officer responsible for the financial statements was on long-term leave; other team members experienced delays in responding. Working papers were not provided within agreed timescales and were below expected quality standards.
findings.matters: This is not a one-off audit delay: it is a systemic weakness that prevents the council meeting statutory financial reporting deadlines. It directly threatens the council's ability to restore timely audited financial reporting and to meet future audit deadlines.
findings.figures: Identified as significant weakness; impacts ability to meet 27 February 2026 backstop date and future deadlines
findings.quote: The Council lacked the necessary expertise and capacity within its Finance Team to appropriately support the external audit process, specifically in its ability to produce supporting working papers and evidence required for the audit. Working papers and supporting evidence were not provided in line with the agreed timetable and did not meet the expected quality requirements.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridge City Council - Audit Results Report February 2026
findings.headline: Material asset misstatements totalling at least £17.84 million across PPE and Investment Property
findings.detail: Four material misstatements were identified: land revaluations not updated in the Fixed Asset Register, understating PPE by £10.61 million; two car parks (Grafton East and West) incorrectly recognised as council-owned assets, overstating PPE by £6.78 million; an investment property fair value not updated, understating IP by £0.395 million; and a valuer using an incorrect income figure, overstating another IP by £0.190 million. The largest issue is the council capitalising assets it does not own.
findings.matters: Large balances are being misstated in the balance sheet. The council cannot verify asset ownership, suggesting weak fixed asset register controls and inadequate reconciliation between valuations and records.
findings.figures: £10.61 million PPE understatement; £6.78 million PPE overstatement; £0.395 million IP understatement; £0.190 million IP overstatement; £171 million total Investment Property balance
findings.quote: Land values of a number of assets revalued in 2024/25 were not updated in the Fixed Asset Register (FAR). This resulted to an understatement of PPE balance by £10.61 million. Our review of the FAR identified that the land values for two assets which are not owned by Council were incorrectly recognised as PPE as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: 25 Cambridge City Council - Audit Results Report February 2026
findings.headline: Third consecutive year auditors cannot issue an opinion on the financial statements
findings.detail: Ernst & Young are disclaiming their audit opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements, following disclaimers on 2023/24 and 2022/23. They have not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to complete their work before the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026. Delays in receiving audit evidence and inability to complete planned procedures mean the accounts have no independent assurance that they present a true and fair view.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the council's accounts are unaudited. Lenders and the finance director cannot rely on them; there is no external assurance that the financial position is accurately stated.
findings.figures: Disclaimers issued for 2022/23, 2023/24, and anticipated for 2024/25; backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: Because of the significance of the matter described in the basis for disclaimer of opinion section of our report, we have not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an audit opinion on these financial statements.

findings.headline: Governance system overhaul required following external expert criticism
findings.detail: Independent review by Centre for Governance and Scrutiny found council's hybrid governance system had significant weaknesses. Council redesigning to Leader and Cabinet model implemented from May 2025. External review highlighted that current arrangements were resource-heavy, opaque, and did not result in improved outcomes.
findings.matters: External expert assessment identified systemic governance weaknesses; transition to new system introduces implementation risk during reorganisation period
findings.figures: Implementation date: May 2025
findings.quote: Their report highlighted the risk that the Council's current arrangements could lead to a lack of collective democratic accountability, was resource heavy, opaque, did not result in improved outcomes for the Council and was not as inclusive as it could be for residents to engage with.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing referral for compliance breaches
findings.detail: Council self-referred to regulator when housing compliance issues were identified and documented. Regulator has issued a judgement and noted improvement plan. Council in regular contact with regulator updating progress. Demonstrated significant improvements in compliance work since referral.
findings.matters: Regulatory oversight indicates governance and compliance weaknesses in a material service area; shows need for intensive monitoring
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: We proactively took legal advice and proactively engaged with the Regulator for Social Housing when we identified that these issues had historically been set and displayed incorrectly.

findings.headline: Housing rent calculation errors requiring tenant refunds and remediation policy
findings.detail: Council identified errors in how service charges were calculated for some tenants. Rents were corrected from April 2024 onwards. Council is now examining individual rent accounts to determine historical overcharges and has established a Rent Regulation Error Refund / Remediation Policy. A separate affordable rent tenancy issue also identified affecting a small number of tenants. In regular contact with DWP on individual cases.
findings.matters: Creates a contingent liability affecting HRA finances; scale of remediation costs not yet quantified in this statement
findings.figures: Multiple tenants affected; specific amounts not disclosed
findings.quote: In late 2023, the Council identified an error in how some of its tenants' rents have been calculated in the past, in relation to some service charges, meaning that affected tenants' rents would need to be corrected going forward, and that some tenants will need to be refunded.

findings.headline: General Fund receives modest net positive interest income, with surplus transferred to earmarked development reserve
findings.detail: Both development and equity loans generate interest income at rates above the council's average investment return. Any interest income above the average return is transferred to an earmarked reserve for development activity. The paper emphasises the primary purpose is housing delivery, not financial return.
findings.matters: The council is treating this partly as a commercial investment (capturing the income spread), but also managing expectations that this is not a profit centre. The mechanism of transferring surplus interest to a development reserve commits future income to further schemes.
findings.figures: Interest income exceeds average investment return rate; no specific quantum stated
findings.quote: Both the development and equity loans will generate interest income at rates higher than the council's current average investment return rate. In accordance with agreed past practice, any additional interest income generated over and above the average investment return rate will be transferred to an earmarked reserve for use to fund other development activity within the city.

findings.headline: Loans are secured by charge against CIP assets, but as asset values increase through development spending, security improves
findings.detail: The £18.5m development loans are secured by charge against CIP's assets. Because the loans fund capital development works, and the development increases asset value as the loan is drawn down and spent, the security position should improve over time. However, CIP performance on these three schemes is the primary determinant of recovery risk.
findings.matters: For a lender, understanding how security evolves matters. Here the security position is dynamic — improving as the development progresses — which mitigates default risk on paper, but only if the developments perform. If a scheme stalls or values decline, security evaporates.
findings.figures: £18.5m development loans secured against assets; £4.677m equity also at risk
findings.quote: Loan facilities will fund development works which are capital in nature, so as the loan is drawn down and spent, the value of assets against which it is secured can be expected to increase.

findings.headline: Interest rates set at 3.5% above 5-year UK gilt rate, with external treasury advisor validation
findings.detail: Development loans will charge 3.5% above the prevailing 5-year UK gilt rate (to be set at each drawdown date). Equity loans charge a notional 5%. This follows advice from MUFG Corporate Markets and is designed to ensure compliance while providing a modest return to the General Fund.
findings.matters: This is a material borrowing decision by the council. The interest rates reflect current market conditions and represent the council's pricing of risk to CIP. The fact that external advisors validated this approach is relevant to assessing governance quality.
findings.figures: 3.5% margin above 5-year gilt rate; 5% notional rate on equity; interest income higher than council's average investment return rate
findings.quote: it is proposed that interest rates on the development loan facilities are set at a margin of 3.5% above the prevailing 5 year UK gilt rate, to be set no later than the date of each drawdown

findings.headline: External subsidy control compliance review was required because of the Subsidy Control Act 2022
findings.detail: In late 2024, Cambridge appointed MUFG Corporate Markets to review the proposed development funding and evaluate subsidy control implications following changes in public sector lending rules. External legal advice from Freeths was also obtained. This indicates that regulatory change created uncertainty about whether prior lending arrangements still complied with law.
findings.matters: Recent regulatory change forced a review, suggesting there was real risk of non-compliance with the lending arrangements. This is material to a lender's assessment of Cambridge's governance maturity and regulatory exposure.
findings.figures: MUFG Corporate Markets engaged in late 2024; Freeths providing legal advice
findings.quote: There has been considerable change in public sector lending rules since prior funding arrangements were agreed between the council and CIP, including changes set out in the Subsidy Control Act 2022. Given the above, the Council in late 2024 appointed its treasury management advisers, MUFG Corporate Markets, to complete a review of proposed development funding, to evaluate the subsidy control implications

findings.headline: Lending limit to Cambridge Investment Partnership increased to £65m for new housing developments not yet completed, concentrating development risk.
findings.detail: The council increased its lending limit to Cambridge Investment Partnership to £65m to accommodate proposed loans for housing at ATS/Murketts, Newbury Farm and Fanshawe Road. These are schemes in delivery, exposing the council to construction and market completion risk.
findings.matters: Development loans to incomplete housing schemes carry construction, market and completion risk; £65m lent to one counterparty amplifies exposure if any scheme falters or the housing market weakens.
findings.figures: CIP lending limit increased to £65m
findings.quote: the limit for lending to Cambridge Investment Partnership LLP (CIP) has been increased to £65 million in order to accommodate proposed loans in respect of approved developments at ATS/Murketts, Newbury Farm and Fanshawe Road

findings.headline: Interest rate cuts ahead will erode investment income: Bank rate is now 4% and forecast to fall to 3.25%, pressuring future revenue.
findings.detail: The Bank of England cut the base rate to 4% in August 2025. The council's treasury advisors forecast further gradual reductions to 3.25%. The council earned £4.705m in investment income in 2024/25, but this windfall will reverse as rates fall.
findings.matters: Investment income supports the council's revenue budget; falling rates will reduce this income at the precise moment the council has depleted cash reserves and committed to major borrowing.
findings.figures: Bank rate now 4%, forecast to 3.25%; investment income earned £4.705m in 2024/25
findings.quote: Further gradual reductions in Bank Rate to 3.25% are then anticipated, with the important proviso that this is only if inflation and employment data are supportive of such cuts.

findings.headline: Cash reserves depleted sharply from £90m to £47m as the council used internal borrowing to fund capital spending.
findings.detail: Investment deposits fell from £90.191m to £46.588m in one year—a 48% reduction. The council funded £23.892m of capital expenditure from cash balances, aggressively depleting liquidity reserves.
findings.matters: Declining cash reserves reduce financial flexibility and buffer capacity; at £47m, the council has modest liquidity relative to £243m in debt and ongoing capital commitments.
findings.figures: Deposits £90.191m to £46.588m
findings.quote: Deposit balances decreased to £46.588 million due to the use of cash balances to fund capital expenditure (internal borrowing).

findings.headline: Park Street hotel and car park development is financed by £85m in external borrowing: £30m drawn in 2024/25, with £55m more pre-arranged for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council took external borrowing of £30 million during the year for Park Street, with a further £55 million committed for 2025/26. This represents substantial commercial property development exposure concentrated in a single project.
findings.matters: Commercial property development lending carries construction, market, and completion risk; £85m committed to one project creates significant concentration risk.
findings.figures: £30m drawn 2024/25, £55m pre-arranged for 2025/26
findings.quote: During the year, £30 million of external borrowing was drawn down for this purpose, with a further £55 million pre-arranged to be drawn down in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure underperformed budget by nearly half: £115m actual against £220m planned, with the shortfall attributed to project slippage.
findings.detail: The council budgeted £220.192m in capital spending but achieved only £115.068m, a 48% underspend. The paper attributes this to slippage on projects but provides no breakdown of which projects slipped or why.
findings.matters: Large capital slippage signals either project delivery risk or strategic reordering; either matters to lenders assessing the council's execution capability and financial planning.
findings.figures: Budget £220.192m, actual £115.068m
findings.quote: Total capital expenditure in 2024/25 was £115.068 million, which was less than the budgeted £220.192 million, largely as a result of slippage on projects.

findings.headline: Grafton Centre East car park revenue fallen by £224k from retail/entertainment closures with warning of further deterioration
findings.detail: Grafton East underperforms by £224k due to 'closure of retail units and the cinema.' The council flags forward risk: 'Although Grafton West is currently on track, the recent cinema closure may soon impact footfall there too' with 'permanent reduction in parking capacity once the neighbouring redevelopment completes, which will require further review of the operating model.'
findings.matters: Commercial income loss from external factors indicates dependence on third-party retail anchors; council is explicitly flagging risk of further deterioration.
findings.figures: £224k Grafton East shortfall
findings.quote: Grafton East is predicting a £224k net shortfall, largely due to the closure of retail units and the cinema. Although Grafton West is currently on track, the recent cinema closure may soon impact footfall there too

findings.headline: HRA rental income shortfall of £150k from higher voids and arrears, with council identifying limited recovery options
findings.detail: HRA dwelling income is £150k below budget from 'higher than budgeted levels of voids and rent arrears.' The council notes recovery is constrained: 'recovering costs is increasingly difficult due to the circumstances and vulnerabilities of many tenants vacating our homes' and acknowledges this is 'widely shared across the social housing sector.'
findings.matters: Rising arrears and voids indicate tenant affordability stress or stock quality issues; constrained recovery means income loss is difficult to reverse.
findings.figures: £150k HRA dwellings income underachievement; voids costs overspent by £193k
findings.quote: An underachievement of £150k is forecast on HRA dwellings income, owing to higher than budgeted levels of voids and rent arrears

findings.headline: Crematorium income down 25% year-on-year due to structural market shift, not temporary underperformance
findings.detail: Despite previous downward budget adjustment, the council forecasts a further £343k decline (25% year-on-year). The council attributes this to 'increased local competition, more affordable online services, and changing consumer preferences' and explicitly states 'These shifts reflect wider trends rather than service-specific performance issues.'
findings.matters: This is a structural revenue decline that will not reverse, indicating a service income line that has materially underperformed against baseline assumptions.
findings.figures: 25% year-on-year reduction (£343k); optional/commemorative services down £39k
findings.quote: the service remains under pressure, with a projected 25% year-on-year reduction (£343k) in income. The market has shifted due to increased local competition, more affordable online services, and changing consumer preferences

findings.headline: HRA capital slippage of £51.3m with explicit flag that overspends will force additional borrowing
findings.detail: Major capital schemes are delayed: East Road (£10.1m), Princess & Hanover (£7.7m), East Barnwell (£6.2m). The council explicitly flags: 'If HRA overspends persist and are not mitigated, less money available for capital spend (including new build), leading to more borrowing.'
findings.matters: Capital slippage combined with revenue overspends creates refinancing pressure; council is flagging borrowing as the consequence of not controlling HRA costs.
findings.figures: £51.3m total capital slippage; £45.867m carry forward requested from Economy and Place
findings.quote: If HRA overspends persist and are not mitigated, less money available for capital spend (including new build), leading to more borrowing.

findings.headline: Damp and mould remediation costs of £555k indicate persistent housing stock condition issue
findings.detail: Responsive Repairs show a £555k overspend because 'the increase is largely due to the volume and complexity of damp and mould cases being addressed.' The council notes this reflects sector-wide pressures: 'our response is consistent with other providers in ensuring homes meet modern health and safety standards.'
findings.matters: Volume and complexity of cases suggests systemic stock condition rather than isolated repairs, indicating future pressure will persist.
findings.figures: £555k responsive repairs overspend
findings.quote: the increase is largely due to the volume and complexity of damp and mould cases being addressed

findings.headline: Fire safety and security compliance spending of £562k driven by regulatory expectations and recent legislation
findings.detail: Asset Management reports a £562k overspend for 'essential fire safety works and building security measures, aligned with national priorities on resident safety and strengthened regulatory expectations following recent legislation and guidance.' These are non-discretionary costs.
findings.matters: Compliance costs are mandatory and likely persistent; they signal either a pre-existing maintenance backlog or ongoing regulatory tightening.
findings.figures: £562k fire safety and security overspend
findings.quote: essential fire safety works and building security measures, aligned with national priorities on resident safety and strengthened regulatory expectations following recent legislation and guidance

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account £1.876m overspend will deplete reserves by £864k instead of increasing them by £1.012m
findings.detail: The HRA forecast overspend swings the reserve position by £1.876m from planned. The council states: 'The overspend would lead to a reduction of £864k in the HRA balance rather than the planned increase of £1.012m.' This deterioration indicates the HRA is consuming financial flexibility rather than building it.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion constrains the council's buffer for unexpected pressures and capital investment, and is a material factor in creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £1.876m forecast overspend; HRA balance falls to -£864k instead of planned +£1.012m
findings.quote: The overspend would lead to a reduction of £864k in the HRA balance rather than the planned increase of £1.012m.

news_drafts.headline: Homes England strategic partnership bid outcome pending, with £2.5m reserve set aside for local government reorganisation transitional costs but actual costs remain highly uncertain
news_drafts.lead: HRA financial plan hinges on grant funding from uncertain bid outcome. LGR transitional costs are contingent and could exceed reserve if staff turnover accelerates or labour market tightens.

news_drafts.headline: Review of asset compliance across operational estate likely to identify significant unbudgeted immediate capital works requirements
news_drafts.lead: Unquantified but material capital demands emerging outside the planned capital programme threaten both borrowing capacity and financial sustainability.

news_drafts.headline: Business rates income shortfall of £1.0m in 2025-26 outturn, with baseline reset removing all previously accumulated growth and significant revaluation appeals pending
news_drafts.lead: Business rates are a core revenue source; a £1m actual shortfall against budget signals either forecast error or volatile income stream. Future growth potential uncertain following baseline reset.
